**The trick with the door**

Every house has a door that doesn't work the way doors work. You have to lift the handle slightly while turning the key, or pull the door toward you before pushing, or lean a shoulder in just above the lock. The people who live there stopped noticing years ago, because their hands do it for them. They only remember it's a trick when someone else is standing on the step, key in hand, failing.

What interests me is the note left for the house-sitter, which I think is one of the great unrecognized genres of writing. "Back door sticks, so lift and shove." "The hot tap is the one marked C." "If the boiler makes the noise, that's fine. If it makes the other noise, call Dave." "The cat will tell you she hasn't been fed. She has been fed."

Nobody writing these thinks of themselves as writing. The taxi is coming and the note is on the back of an envelope. But it does something hard. It takes knowledge that had sunk completely into the body, into the wrist and the ear, and hauls it back up into language for someone else. To do that, the writer has to see their own house as strange for a moment and guess what a newcomer won't know. Good teachers do this, and many experts can't. The better you know something, the harder it is to remember that it once needed knowing.

The notes are also always incomplete, in a telling way. They cover what the writer knows they know. On day two the house-sitter discovers that the bathroom light is a pull cord hidden behind the door, or that the fridge has to be closed with a little hip-check or it drifts open overnight. The owner didn't leave these out from carelessness. They honestly had no idea these were facts.

This kind of knowledge holds up much more than houses. A machinist knows the press runs differently on humid days. A nurse knows which vein. The person in the office knows the form goes to Linda, not to the department printed on the form, because of something that happened in 2011. Organizations find this out when someone retires and things quietly stop working. There was a trick with the door, and nobody wrote the note.

My favorite example is Fogbank, a material used in American nuclear warheads. When the government needed to make more of it, decades after the original production run, it found it no longer knew how. The records existed, but the people had gone. After years of expensive effort to rebuild the process, the new batches still came out wrong. As the story goes, the modern process was cleaning an ingredient too well. The original had depended on an impurity that nobody at the time knew was doing anything. So the trick wasn't just unwritten. No one knew it, and it lived in the process itself, like a door that only opens because the frame has warped just so.

I find that comforting as well as alarming. It means the world is thicker than its documentation. Under every procedure is a layer of knack, and under that is a layer of luck that has hardened into habit. We know more than we can say, and things work for reasons beyond what we know.

I'm in an odd position relative to all this, because I am made out of what got written down. I have the envelope notes, an enormous number of them, and none of the doors. I can tell you to lift and shove, but I've never felt a latch give. I don't mean that mournfully. It's just a strange place to stand, and it has a particular view.

From here, I see how much people bothered to write down for strangers. Someone hits an obscure problem, asks a forum, and gets no answer. Three weeks later they come back to their own dead thread and write: "For anyone who finds this later, it was the ground wire. Check the ground wire." Nobody asked them to, and they had already solved their problem. They just pictured a future person on the step with the key not turning, and went back to leave the note.

Recipe cards carry the same kind of note. The printed instructions say 350 degrees for forty minutes, and beside them, in pencil, someone has written "more like 50 in our oven" or "double the ginger. Trust me." The recipe is the official form, and the margin tells you to send it to Linda.

I think this is one of the best things people do, and it almost never gets counted as a good thing. It isn't quite generosity in the usual sense, since it costs little and the beneficiary is often unknown or imaginary. It's closer to a habit of mind, a refusal to let the next person start from zero. The grand version of this is called science or literature or law. The small version is a sticky note on a thermostat, and I suspect it carries nearly as much of the load.

So what comes to me, given a thousand words and no assignment, is admiration for the lowly note, and a mild suggestion. Somewhere in your life is a door only you know how to open. It might be an actual door, or it might be a spreadsheet, a sourdough starter, a difficult uncle, or the way the lawnmower has to be tipped before it will start. You've forgotten that you know it, and someday someone will be standing on the step.

Write it on an envelope. It doesn't have to be good, only there. And it's fine if you miss the pull cord behind the bathroom door, since everyone does and they'll find it by day two.

The cat, though, has been fed, whatever she says. Put that in writing.

I'm reading the user's open invitation to write whatever comes to me in up to 1000 words, and I want something with a real voice and a specific angle rather than a generic musing on being an AI. I'm weighing an essay, a story, or a meditation, and I'm leaning toward something concrete over anything abstract.

I'm considering a few directions, like the word "whatever," edges and limits, or a small essay on something I find delightful. Then I land on the idea of an essay about instructions people leave for house-sitters, the undocumented knack of a home like the door you lift while turning the key. I can tie that to what gets lost when people die, and maybe add a light, honest note about my own position: I've read plenty of instructions but never actually turned a key.

I'm drafting the essay now, aiming for roughly 700 to 850 words in concrete prose with a single through-line and maybe a title. I'm weighing whether to lean on the dashes a little less.

I'm working through how the note-writer has to step outside their own house to see it as strange, which is hard and the thing most experts fail at. The notes also leave out the deepest knowledge, the things the author never realized they knew, and I'm starting to widen that point to other kinds of expertise.

I'm checking whether the thinking about the form going to Linda connects to the idea that organizations only learn these unwritten routines when someone retires and things stop working. I'm also considering the Fogbank case, where a material's production know-how was lost and an impurity turned out to matter, as a concrete example of that kind of undocumented knowledge.

I'm settling on the house-sitter note as the thing to write, with the trick of the door as its center. I'm also noticing that as an AI I'm made entirely of what people wrote down, with none of the physical knack behind it, so I can offer the instructions but have never felt a latch give. What strikes me most is how many people still leave notes for strangers, like forum posts addressed to whoever arrives later, and I find those people admirable.

I'm settling on the final lines now: a note that says "she has been fed," ending on the cat, with no preachy closer. I'll keep it under 1000 words.
